name: Espresso
intro: Espresso is coffee at its most concentrated: a small, syrupy shot topped with a golden layer of crema. It tastes bold and slightly sharp, with a sweet, lingering finish when it's dialed in well. Every other drink on this list is built on it.
heroAlt: Engraved line illustration of an espresso in a demitasse cup on a saucer with a spoon

vessel.name: Espresso cup (demitasse), pre-warmed
vessel.note: A small, thick-walled cup holds heat and crema best.

ingredients.note: Freshly ground, ideally roasted within the last 2 to 4 weeks.
By weight this is typically about 36 to 40 g in the cup, because the crema adds volume.

equipment.item: Espresso machine with a double-basket portafilter
equipment.alternative: Moka pot or AeroPress (see home methods)

equipment.item: Burr grinder capable of fine, adjustable settings

dialIn.grind: Fine, like table salt, adjusted until the shot runs in the time window

steps.title: Warm everything up
steps.body: Run a blank shot through the empty portafilter and group head, and warm your cup with hot water. Cold metal and ceramic steal heat from the shot and make it taste sour and thin.
steps.tip: Most machines need 15 to 30 minutes to fully heat up. Be patient.

steps.title: Weigh and grind
steps.body: Grind 18 g of coffee into the portafilter basket. Weighing instead of scooping keeps shots repeatable, and a fine grind gives the water enough resistance to extract properly under pressure.
steps.tip: If you can, grind directly into the basket to avoid a mess and static.

steps.title: Level and tamp
steps.body: Gently level the grounds with your finger or a tap on the counter, then tamp straight down with firm, even pressure. The goal is a flat, level bed so water flows evenly through all of it, not just one channel.
steps.tip: Level matters more than force. Don't twist or hammer.

steps.title: Pull the shot
steps.body: Lock in the portafilter, place your cup on a scale if you have one, and start the shot right away. Aim for roughly 25 to 30 seconds from start to finish, with a steady flow that looks like warm honey.
steps.tip: Gushing in under 20 seconds means grind finer. A dribble past 35 seconds means grind coarser.

steps.title: Taste and adjust
steps.body: Sour and sharp usually means under-extracted, so go finer or increase yield slightly. Harsh, bitter and drying means over-extracted, so go coarser. Change only one thing at a time, and make small grinder steps.
steps.tip: Keep notes. Dialing in is a skill, and it's normal to waste a few shots on a new bag.

steps.title: Serve immediately
steps.body: Crema fades within a minute or two and espresso changes quickly as it cools. Serve and sip right away, or stir gently to blend the crema in first.

homeMethods.note: Makes a strong, concentrated coffee using steam pressure. It's rich and punchy but has no true crema and less body than real espresso. Use a fine-medium grind and medium heat, and stop when it starts to sputter.
Use a fine grind, about 18 g coffee, and roughly 2 to 3 oz of hot water, pressing firmly. It's a clean and strong shot, but it's brewed coffee, so expect no crema and a lighter texture.
A drip or pour-over made at double strength is not espresso, but it can stand in for the base of an Americano-style drink. Expect a thinner, less syrupy cup.

tips: Fresh beans and a good burr grinder make a bigger difference than an expensive machine.
Use filtered water if your tap water is very hard or heavily chlorinated.
Preheating the cup keeps the shot hot longer.
Ideal dose, yield and time vary by coffee and roast, so treat the numbers as a starting point.
commonMistakes: Using pre-ground coffee that is too coarse or stale.
Not weighing the dose, which makes every shot different.
Changing several variables at once while dialing in.
Forgetting to preheat the machine and cup.
Uneven tamping that causes channeling, with fast jets of water and a bitter-sour shot.

variations.name: Ristretto
variations.description: A shorter, more concentrated shot using less water through the same dose. It tastes sweeter and heavier. Exact ratios vary by café.

variations.name: Lungo
variations.description: A longer shot with more water through the same dose. It tastes thinner and more bitter.

variations.name: Single shot
variations.description: Uses a smaller basket and dose. The coaster recipe is the double shot.

history: Espresso machines emerged in Italy in the late 1800s and early 1900s, with several inventors and patents involved, and the modern high-pressure style followed in the mid-20th century. The exact credit for who invented what is debated.

seo.title: How to Make Espresso at Home: Dose, Grind and Timing
seo.description: Learn how to pull a double shot of espresso with 18 g of coffee, plus honest alternatives using a moka pot or AeroPress if you don't own a machine.
